description: Countries meet aspirational targets including NDCs and net zero pledges.
pathwayDescription: The Announced Pledges Scenario (APS) provides a pathway in which all countries achieve their aspirational energy transition goals, including national and regional net zero emissions pledges, in addition to their currently legislated policies. As an exploratory scenario, APS provides a detailed description of a possible future, but does not attempt to predict which announced policies will be implemented. The APS pathway corresponds to 1.7°C of warming by 2100 (50% probability). This is significantly lower than the IEA’s current policies scenario (STEPS), which forecasts 2.4°C of warming by 2100 (50% probability), but still higher than the IEA’s Net Zero scenario (NZE), which targets 1.5°C of warming by 2100 (50% probability). This indicates that the policies and pledges incorporated into APS significantly increase the pace of the transition compared to status quo conditions.

coreDrivers.policies: The APS assumes current nationally determined contributions (NDCs) are met, including emissions intensity goals and coal phase-out commitments. Carbon pricing widens and steepens, reaching USD 200/t CO2 by 2050 in advanced economies with net zero pledges and USD 160/t CO2 in selected emerging economies, phase-out and retirement instruments are more binding with coal-fired generation down more than 50% by 2035 and early retirement of coal plants accelerating.
coreDrivers.emissionsTargets: The APS pathway assumes governments meet all climate commitments, including Nationally Determined Contributions and longer-term net zero emissions targets, in full and on time.
coreDrivers.technologyCosts: Unit technology costs are endogenous and deployment-linked: future cost evolution is tied to deployment levels, following a non-linear learning curve.
coreDrivers.investmentChange: The shift toward low-carbon investment is substantially larger than in the corresponding IEA STEPS pathway. Average annual total investment rises from USD 3 785.2 billion in 2024-2030 to USD 4 430.0 billion in 2041-2050, while the fossil component falls from USD 863.1 to USD 363.0 billion, taking the fossil share from about 23% to about 8%.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: Population follows the UN medium variant, reaching 9.68 billion in 2050, and GDP grows from USD 175,981 billion to USD 357,510 billion (2023, PPP).

dependencies.dependency_description: This pathway is defined by the assumption that pledged policy is delivered in full and on time, so policy strategy is the main enabling condition for every lever. Carbon pricing is extended to all regions with net zero pledges while sub-Saharan Africa excluding South Africa and developing Asia are assumed to rely on direct policy interventions instead, so the dependency falls on different instruments in different regions.

Transmission and distribution investment reaches USD 944.7 billion a year in 2041-2050, and battery storage 4,386 GW by 2050, all of it subject to the decade-long project lead times and connection queues the publication identifies. Market-design reform is explicitly called for alongside the investment, not just the investment itself.

The fossil share of average annual energy investment has to fall from about 23% in 2024-2030 to about 8% in 2041-2050 while total investment rises to USD 4 430 billion a year. Carbon prices of USD 200/t CO2 in advanced economies and USD 160/t CO2 in China, India and Indonesia are the main mechanism making the hydrogen and CCUS levers bankable; where no explicit pricing is assumed, the levers rely on direct intervention instead.

Nuclear and hydro capacity rises, both technologies with well-known siting and acceptance histories, while grid expansion runs ahead of the corresponding IEA STEPS pathway. The publication does not analyse acceptance for these technologies, so the elevated rating rests on the deployment differential rather than on any stated finding.

The end-use electrification is the largest lever in this pathway and it runs through household and firm purchasing decisions. Sustainable aviation fuels reach 5% of aviation energy demand by 2030, which depends on airline and customer willingness to absorb a fuel premium. Frictions affect the pathway: rural charging availability, and heat pump paybacks of a decade or more against falling but still material upfront costs.

Network investment 2.4 times current levels and battery investment five times, with storage reaching 4 386 GW by 2050 and transmission and distribution investment at USD 944.7 billion a year in 2041-2050. Interconnection matters because the early retirement of coal plants shifts adequacy onto storage and system flexibility, some of it from demand-side management.

Captured CO2 rises to 3 731 Mt by 2050, low-emissions hydrogen production to 24.9 EJ, and BECCS at 481 TWh of generation however all of which require market readiness that the publication treats as an assumption rather than a fact.

The mineral dependency scales with deployment, against the same stated risk of supply shortages and price spikes if mineral investment does not keep pace. Bioenergy needs also rise sharply, with modern solid bioenergy supply at 72.9 EJ and liquid biofuels at 13.9 EJ against 56.1 and 8.2 EJ, and no land-availability constraint is quantified anywhere in the publication, so that increment is unassessed.

No climate impact constrains any lever in this pathway either and no resilience or adaptation measure is quantified; the increased reliance on hydropower, is not paired with any hydrological assessment.

The fossil supply employment turns from growth to contraction while clean energy recruitment accelerates. The publication notes that even highly skilled oil and gas workers face geographic and remuneration barriers to switching, and that coal workers face particular difficulty because their skills do not align neatly with other energy jobs. The shortage of trade workers and of qualified grid staff constrains delivery of the electrification lever directly.
